title: Accessible Computer Science for K-12 Students with Hearing Impairments
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of accessible computer science instruction for K-12 students who are Deaf or hard of hearing (D/HH), with particular attention to students who use American Sign Language (ASL). The authors argue that many existing resources are not well suited to D/HH learners because captions can be inaccurate or linguistically too difficult, and because technical STEM vocabulary often lacks accessible ASL explanations. The paper is motivated by equity and inclusion concerns and by the need to better support D/HH students’ participation in computing education.

The paper presents an early-stage project to develop an accessible block-based computer science learning environment. The approach combines ASL video explanations of core programming concepts (for example, loops, variables, functions, and debugging) with captions, tooltips, and other accessibility features embedded in a block-based web application. The system is intended to support both D/HH students and their teachers, including hearing educators and sign interpreters, by providing accurate ASL representations of technical terms and interactive visual feedback within coding activities.

The context is middle-school and broader K-12 education in the United States, especially for D/HH learners who may have limited access to teachers fluent in ASL or to appropriate STEM sign vocabulary. The paper does not report an empirical evaluation of learning outcomes; instead, it outlines design rationale, accessibility heuristics, and planned future work, including a forthcoming study with middle-school deaf students. The main conclusion is that accessible, multimodal, ASL-supported coding materials are needed to make introductory computer science more inclusive and understandable for D/HH learners.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/design paper describing an accessibility project and future plans, not an empirical evaluation. There is no study design, control group, or outcome data reported.
impact_tier_rationale: The potential relevance to priority populations is high, especially for Deaf/Hard of Hearing K-12 students, but the paper reports no measured impact. The expected benefit is plausible yet unquantified, so the impact tier is modest/unclear.

interventions.use_case: accessible block-based computer science instruction for K-12 Deaf/Hard of Hearing students using ASL video explanations, captions, tooltips, and interactive coding tutorials
robot-supported programming activities where students use block code to control a cost-effective educational robot as part of the inclusive CS curriculum

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes an accessible block-based CS curriculum for middle-school D/HH students, with ASL video explanations of core programming concepts (e.g., variables, loops, debugging) and robot-based activities. No learning outcomes are empirically reported yet; the paper is a design/proposal describing the intervention intended to improve access to computer science concepts for D/HH learners.
finding.measure: proposed accessibility and curriculum design; no student outcome measured

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that ASL-based instruction, captions, and multimodal supports will increase students' excitement about CS, sense of inclusion, and motivation to learn independently. These are hypothesized benefits rather than measured effects, so no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: proposed inclusion, excitement, motivation, and independent learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that reusable ASL videos and built-in accessibility features could reduce reliance on teachers/interpreters to explain core CS terminology and provide consistent access to content. This is a design rationale only; the paper does not measure teacher workload or efficiency outcomes.
finding.measure: anticipated teacher/support burden and content reusability

finding.finding_summary: The work focuses on expanding equitable access to K-12 CS for Deaf/Hard of Hearing students and on creating accessibility requirements for a broader inclusive web application. It frames the intervention as a pathway to improve participation of underrepresented students in STEM, but provides no empirical institutional outcome data.
finding.measure: equity/accessibility goals for D/HH K-12 CS participation
